not_good_for.text: Asthma / COPD: Fine particle pollution (PM2.5), Very hot days and Muggy days

verdict_rule: High risk if any main factor is red · Caution if any is yellow · otherwise Suitable. Trend-only cards (no limit) don't change the verdict.

notable_years.text: 2005: Traffic & industry pollution (NO₂), Fire detections nearby and Haze (aerosol optical depth) were all unusually bad that year.
2009: Summer ground heat (5 km) and Neighborhood surface heat were both unusually bad that year.

2011: Very hot days, Warm nights, Dangerous heat-index days, Haze (aerosol optical depth), Summer ground heat (5 km), Water storage (ground, soil, snow) and Neighborhood surface heat were all unusually bad that year.
2017: Heavy rain days, Frost-free season and Fire detections nearby were all unusually bad that year.
2022: Very hot days, Warm nights, Dangerous heat-index days, Smoke days, Summer ground heat (5 km) and Neighborhood surface heat were all unusually bad that year.
2023: Very hot days, Warm nights, Dangerous heat-index days and Smoke days were all unusually bad that year.

hot_days.label: Very hot days
hot_days.data_source: NASA POWER (MERRA-2) daily max temperature T2M_MAX, ~50 km grid
hot_days.definition: Days when the temperature reaches 35 °C (95 °F) or more.
hot_days.caveat: NASA POWER averages a ~50 km square, and its daily highs run about 1 °C cooler than weather stations, so a nearby station usually counts more 95 °F days than this card. Trust the trend more than the count.

limits.source: 95 °F is one of the fixed hot-day levels (90, 95, 100, 105 °F) used in US environmental public health tracking; 30 and 60 days (about one and two months a year) are team-defined.

story.happened: Very hot days: 36 days a year on average in 2001–2005, compared with 79 days a year in 2021–2025.
story.is_it_real: The trend is +19.5 days per decade (95% CI +0.8 to +36.7), but not statistically significant yet (p = 0.040): it could still be normal year-to-year ups and downs. A longer record may settle it.
story.why_it_matters: People 65 and older, and people with chronic conditions, are more prone to heat-related illness.
story.what_it_likely_means: No clear direction: most years fell in the usual range of about 18–98 days.

overall.method: Seasonal Kendall, corrected for month-to-month memory

warm_nights.label: Warm nights
warm_nights.data_source: NASA POWER (MERRA-2) daily min temperature T2M_MIN, ~50 km grid
warm_nights.definition: Nights when the temperature stays at 24 °C (75 °F) or above.
warm_nights.caveat: This ~50 km average misses a city's extra night-time heat (Phoenix airport's nights run about 3 °C warmer than this grid), so the real city is likely worse than this card.

limits.source: NWS HeatRisk counts unusually warm overnight lows as adding to heat stress; the 75 °F level and the 30/90-night cutoffs are team-defined to pick out the warmest US night climates.

story.happened: Warm nights: 41 nights a year on average in 2001–2005, compared with 73 nights a year in 2021–2025.
story.is_it_real: The trend is +15.9 nights per decade (95% CI +6.3 to +26.7) and statistically significant (Mann-Kendall p = 0.004).
story.why_it_matters: Warm nights keep the body from recovering from daytime heat, adding to heat stress the next day.
story.what_it_likely_means: This has been getting worse steadily: 2021–2025 was worse than 2001–2005, so the early years are no longer a good guide to this place.

overall.method: Seasonal Kendall, corrected for month-to-month memory

cold_days.label: Very cold nights
cold_days.data_source: NASA POWER (MERRA-2) daily min temperature T2M_MIN, ~50 km grid
cold_days.caveat: This ~50 km average does not adjust for elevation or cold valleys, so a specific address can see more or fewer very cold nights than shown.

limits.source: Cold causes more US deaths than heat (JAMA Network Open, 2025), but no US agency sets one cold-night health limit, so 10 °F and the 10/30-night cutoffs are team-defined.

story.happened: Very cold nights: none at all in any year from 2001 to 2025.
story.is_it_real: There is no change to test: the value was the same every year.
story.why_it_matters: Long exposure to very cold temperatures can cause hypothermia, which can happen even above 40 °F if a person is wet.
story.what_it_likely_means: This didn't happen here in any year of the record.

overall.method: Seasonal Kendall, corrected for month-to-month memory

heavy_rain_days.label: Heavy rain days
heavy_rain_days.data_source: NASA POWER daily precipitation PRECTOTCORR, ~50 km grid
heavy_rain_days.definition: Days with 20 mm (0.8 in) of rain or more.
heavy_rain_days.caveat: NASA's model spreads rain over too many days and flattens single-day downpours, so it counts fewer heavy-rain days than a rain gauge. Read the trend, not the number.

limits.source: US agencies define heavy rain against each place's own history (its top 1% of days), not one national count, and a 50 km grid smooths local downpours, so this card shows the trend only.

story.happened: Heavy rain days: 18 days a year on average in 2001–2005, compared with 12 days a year in 2021–2025.
story.is_it_real: The trend is -2.6 days per decade (95% CI -6.0 to +0.9), but not statistically significant yet (p = 0.14): it could still be normal year-to-year ups and downs. A longer record may settle it.
story.why_it_matters: Flooding and water damage can lead to damp and mould at home.
story.what_it_likely_means: No clear direction: most years fell in the usual range of about 8–22 days.

source.name: US EPA — A Brief Guide to Mold, Moisture and Your Home

overall.method: Seasonal Kendall, corrected for month-to-month memory

dry_days.label: Very dry days
dry_days.data_source: NASA POWER (MERRA-2) relative humidity RH2M, ~50 km grid
dry_days.definition: Days when average humidity is below 20%.
dry_days.caveat: Humidity here is a ~50 km model average that has not been checked against local stations, so read the trend, not the exact count.

limits.source: There is no US health limit for outdoor humidity; NWS fire-weather warnings start near 15% humidity together with strong wind, so this card shows the trend only.

story.happened: Very dry days: none at all in any year from 2001 to 2025.
story.is_it_real: There is no change to test: the value was the same every year.
story.why_it_matters: Very dry air can dry the eyes and skin, and dry, windy days raise wildfire danger.
story.what_it_likely_means: This didn't happen here in any year of the record.

source.name: NWS Grand Junction — Fire Weather Criteria

overall.method: Seasonal Kendall, corrected for month-to-month memory

muggy_days.label: Muggy days
muggy_days.data_source: NASA POWER (MERRA-2) dew point T2MDEW, ~50 km grid
muggy_days.definition: Days when the dew point is 21 °C (70 °F) or higher — sticky, humid air.
muggy_days.caveat: Dew point is NASA POWER's most station-like value (within about 0.2 °C on average worldwide), but it is still a ~50 km average.

limits.source: Meteorologists call dew points of 70 °F uncomfortable and 75 °F oppressive; 30 and 90 days are team-defined comfort cutoffs, not a health limit.

story.happened: Muggy days: 120 days a year on average in 2001–2005, compared with 118 days a year in 2021–2025.
story.is_it_real: The trend is +3.5 days per decade (95% CI -7.6 to +17.7), but not statistically significant yet (p = 0.69): it could still be normal year-to-year ups and downs. A longer record may settle it.
story.why_it_matters: Long humid spells help mould grow indoors, a common asthma and allergy trigger.
story.what_it_likely_means: No clear direction: most years fell in the usual range of about 92–138 days.

source.name: US EPA — A Brief Guide to Mold, Moisture and Your Home

overall.method: Seasonal Kendall, corrected for month-to-month memory

humid_heat_days.label: Humid-heat days
humid_heat_days.data_source: NASA POWER (MERRA-2) daily-mean wet-bulb temperature T2MWET, ~50 km grid
humid_heat_days.definition: Days when the air is so hot and humid that sweat stops cooling the body well (daily-mean wet-bulb of 24 °C or more).
humid_heat_days.caveat: A ~50 km grid average of the whole day; afternoons are worse, and city streets hold more heat.

limits.source: Trend only: there is no US health limit for a yearly count of humid-heat days.

story.happened: Humid-heat days: 108 days a year on average in 2001–2005, compared with 121 days a year in 2021–2025.
story.is_it_real: The trend is +6.9 days per decade (95% CI +2.0 to +12.7) and statistically significant (Mann-Kendall p = 0.008).
story.why_it_matters: Older adults, young children and people with heart disease are most affected by humid heat (CDC).
story.what_it_likely_means: This has been getting worse steadily: 2021–2025 was worse than 2001–2005, so the early years are no longer a good guide to this place.

overall.method: Seasonal Kendall, corrected for month-to-month memory

heat_index_days.label: Dangerous heat-index days
heat_index_days.data_source: NASA POWER (MERRA-2) daily max temperature T2M_MAX and dew point T2MDEW, ~50 km grid
heat_index_days.definition: Days when heat and humidity together feel like 103 °F or more at the hottest time of day, the National Weather Service's Danger level.
heat_index_days.caveat: Worked out from the day's highest temperature and its average dew point on a ~50 km grid; the heat index is measured in shade, and full sun can add up to 15 °F.

limits.source: Trend only: the National Weather Service's Danger level is for a single day, not a yearly count.

story.happened: Dangerous heat-index days: 40 days a year on average in 2001–2005, compared with 81 days a year in 2021–2025.
story.is_it_real: The trend is +20.0 days per decade (95% CI +7.0 to +32.2) and statistically significant (Mann-Kendall p = 0.002).
story.why_it_matters: At this level heat cramps and heat exhaustion are likely, and heat stroke is possible with long exposure or activity (National Weather Service). Older adults, young children and people with heart disease are most at risk (CDC).
story.what_it_likely_means: This has been getting worse steadily: 2021–2025 was worse than 2001–2005, so the early years are no longer a good guide to this place.

overall.method: Seasonal Kendall, corrected for month-to-month memory

wettest_day.label: Wettest day of the year
wettest_day.data_source: NASA POWER daily precipitation PRECTOTCORR, ~50 km grid
wettest_day.definition: The most rain that fell in a single day each year.
wettest_day.caveat: NASA's model spreads rain over too many days and flattens single-day downpours, so it counts fewer heavy-rain days than a rain gauge. Read the trend, not the number.

limits.source: US agencies define heavy rain against each place's own history (its top 1% of days), not one national count, and a 50 km grid smooths local downpours, so this card shows the trend only.

story.happened: Wettest day of the year: 69 mm on average in 2001–2005, compared with 53 mm in 2021–2025.
story.is_it_real: The trend is -7.7 mm per decade (95% CI -20.7 to +6.5), but not statistically significant yet (p = 0.39): it could still be normal year-to-year ups and downs. A longer record may settle it.
story.why_it_matters: The biggest single-day downpours are the ones most likely to cause local flooding.
story.what_it_likely_means: No clear direction: most years fell in the usual range of about 45–108 mm.

overall.method: Seasonal Kendall, corrected for month-to-month memory

frost_free_season.label: Frost-free season
frost_free_season.unit: days between last spring and first fall frost
frost_free_season.data_source: NASA POWER (MERRA-2) daily min temperature T2M_MIN, ~50 km grid
frost_free_season.definition: The number of days between the last frost of spring and the first frost of fall (nights at 32 °F or colder).
frost_free_season.caveat: Night lows on a ~50 km grid; valleys and open fields frost earlier than city centres. Left empty where frost comes in fewer than four years out of five.

limits.source: Trend only: a longer frost-free season means a longer pollen season and more time for ticks and mosquitoes; there is no health limit for its length.

story.happened: Frost-free season: 297 days a year on average in 2001–2005, compared with 280 days a year in 2018–2025.
story.is_it_real: The trend is -2.0 days per decade (95% CI -20.0 to +15.0), but not statistically significant yet (p = 0.80): it could still be normal year-to-year ups and downs. A longer record may settle it.
story.why_it_matters: A longer frost-free season gives plants more time to release pollen and gives ticks and mosquitoes longer to be active.
story.what_it_likely_means: No clear direction: most years fell in the usual range of about 271–318 days.

pm25.label: Fine particle pollution (PM2.5)
pm25.data_source: NASA MERRA-2 aerosol diagnostics M2TMNXAER (monthly), PM2.5 rebuilt from dust, sea salt, sulfate, black and organic carbon (no nitrate), ~50 km grid; from 2010, because the model's fire-smoke input changed that year and its PM2.5 jumps in 2009–10 where EPA ground monitors fell (D41)
pm25.definition: Tiny particles in the air, 2.5 micrometres or smaller, from smoke, traffic, industry and dust.
pm25.caveat: NASA's MERRA-2 PM2.5 is a 50 km model estimate without nitrate, so it reads lower than city monitors, especially in winter. Trust the direction of the trend more than the number. It starts in 2010: the model changed how it adds fire smoke that year, and its earlier years read too low where fires matter.

limits.source: official: US EPA primary annual standard (2024), upheld by the D.C. Circuit in June 2026
limits.high_source: official: US EPA secondary annual standard and WHO interim target 3 (15 µg/m³)

story.happened: Fine particle pollution (PM2.5): 12.8 µg/m³ on average in 2010–2014, compared with 12.8 µg/m³ in 2021–2025.
story.is_it_real: The trend is -0.0 µg/m³ per decade (95% CI -0.8 to +1.2), but not statistically significant yet (p = 1.00): it could still be normal year-to-year ups and downs. A longer record may settle it.
story.why_it_matters: Fine particles can get deep into the lungs, and some into the bloodstream, affecting the lungs and heart and aggravating asthma.
story.what_it_likely_means: No clear direction: most years fell in the usual range of about 12.4–14.2 µg/m³.

source.name: US EPA — Health and Environmental Effects of Particulate Matter

overall.method: Seasonal Kendall, corrected for month-to-month memory

no2.label: Traffic & industry pollution (NO₂)
no2.data_source: NASA OMI/Aura tropospheric NO2 column OMNO2d (daily, 0.25° ≈ 25 km), 2005 onward; the team files' version (003 or 004) is not yet confirmed (D10)
no2.definition: Nitrogen dioxide, a gas mainly from traffic, power plants and industry, measured from space by NASA's OMI instrument.
no2.caveat: Satellite NO2 measures the whole air column above your area, not the air you breathe. It shows whether traffic and industry pollution is rising or falling, and since about 2010 it understates how much street-level NO2 has dropped.

limits.source: none: there is no official health limit for satellite NO2 columns, so this card shows the trend only

story.happened: Traffic & industry pollution (NO₂): 6.33 ×10¹⁵ molec/cm² on average in 2005–2009, compared with 4.70 ×10¹⁵ molec/cm² in 2021–2025.
story.is_it_real: The trend is -0.89 ×10¹⁵ molec/cm² per decade (95% CI -1.61 to -0.43) and statistically significant (Mann-Kendall p < 0.001).
story.why_it_matters: NO₂ inflames the airways; longer exposure may contribute to asthma developing.
story.what_it_likely_means: This has been improving steadily: 2021–2025 was better than 2005–2009.

source.name: US EPA — Basic Information about NO2

overall.method: Seasonal Kendall, corrected for month-to-month memory

fires.label: Fire detections nearby
fires.data_source: NASA FIRMS MODIS active fires (Terra + Aqua, C6.1, 1 km; vegetation type 0, confidence >= 30 = nominal + high); trend from 2003
fires.definition: Satellite fire detections within 50 km, including farm and prescribed burns.
fires.caveat: Each detection is a 1 km pixel where NASA's MODIS saw a fire at least once. Small, short or cloud-hidden fires are missed and farm and prescribed burns are counted. In oil and gas fields, such as West Texas, many detections are gas flares, not wildfires. So this shows how fire activity nearby changed, not the number of fires or acres burned. Trend from 2003, when the second satellite joined.

limits.source: A detection is a 1 km satellite pixel with one or more fires, often a farm or prescribed burn, and smoke travels far beyond 50 km, so the count shows nearby fire activity as a trend, not a health level.

story.happened: Fire detections nearby: 58 detections a year on average in 2003–2007, compared with 61 detections a year in 2021–2025.
story.is_it_real: The trend is +0.0 detections per decade (95% CI -15.7 to +14.4), but not statistically significant yet (p = 0.94): it could still be normal year-to-year ups and downs. A longer record may settle it.
story.why_it_matters: Wildfire smoke carries fine particles that worsen asthma, COPD and heart disease, and is a risk in pregnancy.
story.what_it_likely_means: No clear direction: most years fell in the usual range of about 46–92 detections.

source.name: US EPA — Who is at increased risk from wildfire smoke

overall.method: Seasonal Kendall, corrected for month-to-month memory

smoke_days.label: Smoke days
smoke_days.unit: days / year with medium or thick smoke overhead
smoke_days.data_source: NOAA Hazard Mapping System smoke polygons (drawn by analysts from satellite images), medium and heavy outlines only, on the ~50 km MERRA-2 grid; from 2011. Light outlines are left out: that smoke is often high above the ground, and NOAA changed how it labels smoke density in 2022 (Liu et al. 2024, International Journal of Wildland Fire)
smoke_days.definition: Days with medium or thick wildfire smoke drawn over this place on NOAA's satellite smoke maps.
smoke_days.caveat: Counts medium and thick smoke anywhere in the air column, from 2011; on some days it stays high above the ground. Light smoke is left out: it is usually aloft, and NOAA changed how it labels it in 2022. Analysts draw the outlines by hand.

limits.source: Trend only: smoke overhead is not always smoke at ground level, so no health limit applies.

story.happened: Smoke days: 6 days a year on average in 2011–2015, compared with 19 days a year in 2021–2025.
story.is_it_real: The trend is +4.3 days per decade (95% CI -4.0 to +15.0), but not statistically significant yet (p = 0.25): it could still be normal year-to-year ups and downs. A longer record may settle it.
story.why_it_matters: Smoke is hardest on people with asthma or COPD, children and older adults (EPA AirNow).
story.what_it_likely_means: No clear direction: most years fell in the usual range of about 1–22 days.

overall.method: Seasonal Kendall, corrected for month-to-month memory

aod.label: Haze (aerosol optical depth)
aod.data_source: NASA MERRA-2 M2TMNXAER total aerosol extinction (TOTEXTTAU, 550 nm), ~50 km grid
aod.definition: How hazy the whole column of air is: 0.1 is clear, above 0.4 is hazy (smoke, dust, pollution).
aod.caveat: A model estimate for the whole column of air, not what people breathe at the ground.

limits.source: Trend only: optical depth measures haze through the whole air column, not the air people breathe.

story.happened: Haze (aerosol optical depth): 0.208 AOD on average in 2001–2005, compared with 0.184 AOD in 2021–2025.
story.is_it_real: The trend is -0.012 AOD per decade (95% CI -0.021 to -0.006) and statistically significant (Mann-Kendall p = 0.002).
story.what_it_likely_means: This has been improving steadily: 2021–2025 was better than 2001–2005.

overall.method: Seasonal Kendall, corrected for month-to-month memory

rain_sat.label: Rain seen from satellites (IMERG)
rain_sat.data_source: NASA GPM IMERG Final V07 monthly precipitation, ~10 km grid, to September 2025
rain_sat.definition: All rain and melted snow in a year, measured by a network of satellites.
rain_sat.caveat: Satellite estimates miss some light rain and snow; compare with the NASA POWER rain cards.

limits.source: Trend only: a second, satellite-based rain record beside NASA POWER.

story.happened: Rain seen from satellites (IMERG): 1,549 mm on average in 2001–2005, compared with 1,276 mm in 2020–2024.
story.is_it_real: The trend is -123.0 mm per decade (95% CI -295.3 to +118.8), but not statistically significant yet (p = 0.17): it could still be normal year-to-year ups and downs. A longer record may settle it.
story.what_it_likely_means: No clear direction: most years fell in the usual range of about 1,051–1,820 mm.

overall.method: Seasonal Kendall, corrected for month-to-month memory

surface_heat_5km.label: Summer ground heat (5 km)
surface_heat_5km.data_source: NASA MODIS MOD11C3 v061 monthly daytime land-surface temperature (Terra), 0.05° grid; trend to 2022 (orbit drift after)
surface_heat_5km.definition: How hot the ground gets in the summer sun (June to August, late morning), about 5 km squares.
surface_heat_5km.caveat: Ground temperature, not air temperature. Terra's orbit drift makes 2023–2025 read cool, so the trend stops at 2022.

limits.source: Trend only: ground temperature is not air temperature; it shows how hot streets and fields get in the sun.

story.happened: Summer ground heat (5 km): 37.1 °C on average in 2001–2005, compared with 38.5 °C in 2018–2022.
story.is_it_real: The trend is +0.8 °C per decade (95% CI +0.3 to +1.1) and statistically significant (Mann-Kendall p = 0.006).
story.what_it_likely_means: This has been getting worse steadily: 2018–2022 was worse than 2001–2005, so the early years are no longer a good guide to this place.

overall.method: Seasonal Kendall, corrected for month-to-month memory

water_storage.label: Water storage (ground, soil, snow)
water_storage.unit: cm of water vs the 2004–2009 average
water_storage.data_source: NASA/DLR GRACE and GRACE-FO JPL mascons RL06.3 (gravity satellites), ~300 km effective; gap mid-2017 to mid-2018
water_storage.definition: Water stored in the ground, soil and snow, compared with 2004–2009, measured by tiny changes in Earth's gravity.
water_storage.caveat: Regional (about 300 km), so it cannot see one town's wells; there is a gap in mid-2017 to mid-2018.

limits.source: Trend only: a regional water budget; falling means the area is losing stored water.

story.happened: Water storage (ground, soil, snow): 2.1 cm on average in 2003–2007, compared with -7.7 cm in 2021–2025.
story.is_it_real: The trend is -5.6 cm per decade (95% CI -13.4 to +1.0), but not statistically significant yet (p = 0.13): it could still be normal year-to-year ups and downs. A longer record may settle it.
story.what_it_likely_means: No clear direction: most years fell in the usual range of about -15.2–7.7 cm.

overall.method: Seasonal Kendall, corrected for month-to-month memory

surface_heat.label: Neighborhood surface heat
surface_heat.data_source: NASA MODIS/Terra MOD11A2 v061 (8-day, 1 km, ~10:30 am overpass), via ORNL DAAC; trend 2001-2022 because Terra's orbit drifted after 2020
surface_heat.definition: How hot the ground, roofs and roads get on clear summer late mornings, measured by NASA's MODIS satellite at 1 km.
surface_heat.caveat: MODIS measures how hot the ground and roofs get on a clear summer late morning, which is often much hotter than the air you feel. The trend stops in 2022 because the satellite's orbit drifted, which makes later years read artificially cool.

limits.source: No health limit exists for ground temperature, and EPA says air temperature, not surface temperature, best reflects what people feel, so this card shows the trend only.

story.happened: Neighborhood surface heat: 37.0 °C on average in 2001–2005, compared with 38.6 °C in 2018–2022.
story.is_it_real: The trend is +0.9 °C per decade (95% CI +0.4 to +1.5) and statistically significant (Mann-Kendall p = 0.007).
story.why_it_matters: Neighborhoods with more pavement and fewer trees stay hotter, raising heat stress for people living there.
story.what_it_likely_means: This has been getting worse steadily: 2018–2022 was worse than 2001–2005, so the early years are no longer a good guide to this place.

source.name: US EPA — What Are Heat Islands?

heat_island.label: Heat island vs surroundings
heat_island.definition: How much hotter the area around the address is than the wider 11 × 11 km area.
heat_island.caveat: This compares the 3 × 3 km around the address with the 11 × 11 km around it, which is usually also built up, so it is smaller than a city-versus-countryside heat island; in desert cities, irrigated neighborhoods can be cooler than bare ground.

limits.source: Across 38 US cities, built-up land was on average 4.3 °C hotter at the surface than surrounding land on summer days (NASA MODIS, Imhoff et al. 2010), so +4 °C marks a typical city-scale heat island and +2 °C half of it; both cutoffs are team-defined.

story.happened: Heat island vs surroundings: 0.1 °C on average in 2001–2005, compared with 0.1 °C in 2021–2025.
story.is_it_real: The trend is -0.1 °C per decade (95% CI -0.2 to -0.0), but not statistically significant yet (p = 0.042): it could still be normal year-to-year ups and downs. A longer record may settle it.
story.why_it_matters: Urban heat islands add extra heat on top of the regional climate.
story.what_it_likely_means: No clear direction: most years fell in the usual range of about -0.0–0.5 °C.

source.name: US EPA — What Are Heat Islands?

actions.label: Fine particle pollution (PM2.5)
actions: Run a HEPA air purifier sized for the bedroom.
Check the daily air quality index; close windows on bad days.

source.name: US EPA — Health and Environmental Effects of Particulate Matter

actions.label: Very hot days
actions: Choose a home with working air conditioning and a plan for power cuts.
Plan outdoor activity for early morning in the hot season.
Store medicines and inhalers away from heat, as the label says.

actions.label: Warm nights
actions: Keep cooling running overnight during hot spells.
Prefer a bedroom that doesn't face west or sit under the roof.

actions.label: Humid-heat days
actions: Choose a home with working air conditioning and a plan for power cuts.
Plan outdoor activity for early morning in the hot season.

actions.label: Dangerous heat-index days
actions: Choose a home with working air conditioning and a plan for power cuts.
Plan outdoor work and play for early morning on hot, humid days.

actions.label: Neighborhood surface heat
actions: Look for streets with trees and parks nearby.
A light-coloured or well-insulated roof keeps the home cooler.

source.name: US EPA — What Are Heat Islands?

other_checks.label: Radon (US)
other_checks.text: Radon is a radioactive gas from the ground; the only way to know is to test the home.

other_checks.label: Official flood map (US)
other_checks.text: Check the flood zone for the exact address.

other_checks.label: Local safety statistics
other_checks.text: Check your city or police department's official open data.
